articles.title: In 2024, Arizona used foam made from 100% recycled glass at 19 sites while widening 23 miles of I-17; the lightweight fill helped culverts built for two lanes support added lanes
articles.summary: US News: Engineers in Arizona have used an unusual material to expand a major interstate: tens of thousands of tonnes of crushed recycled glass. During the exp.
articles.body: Engineers in Arizona have used an unusual material to expand a major interstate: tens of thousands of tonnes of crushed recycled glass. During the expansion of Interstate 17 north of Phoenix, construction crews used ultra-lightweight foam glass aggregate at 19 locations along a 23-mile section. The material, made entirely from recycled glass, provided a lightweight structural fill that allowed existing drainage culverts, built decades ago for a two-lane highway, to support extra traffic lanes without being crushed by the added weight. According to the Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT), this was the first time foam glass aggregate had been used in a state infrastructure project. In an official agency publication, ADOT Communications representative Laura Douglas said the material was chosen because it combines high compressive strength, low weight and environmental benefits.Solving structural challenges on a busy corridorThe 23-mile section of Interstate 17 between Anthem Way and Sunset Point is one of the region's busiest major routes, carrying more than one million motorists each year. To reduce regular traffic jams and meet growing travel demand, state transport authorities began a major widening project. The work included adding third travel lanes between Anthem Way and Black Canyon City, as well as building dynamic flex lanes through the mountainous area leading to Sunset Point. However, adding lanes meant widening the highway over old concrete box culverts built beneath the road. These underground structures play an important role by carrying stormwater underneath the highway. The original culverts were designed to support only two lanes of traffic. Adding normal soil, stone or heavy concrete fill above them to support wider lanes could have placed too much weight on the structures. Replacing or rebuilding the culverts would have cost much more and caused longer delays in the busy construction area. Engineers found an alternative in ultra-lightweight foam glass aggregate. By using the glass material instead of traditional earth fill, workers reduced the weight placed on the underground concrete boxes.Manufacturing an ultra-lightweight fillAlthough it is made from recycled glass bottles and containers, the finished material looks very different from ordinary glass. "Foam glass is made by crushing recycled glass into a powder and mixing it with a foaming agent," Douglas detailed in the ADOT report. "The mixed powder is then sent through a kiln and softened. During this process, the foaming agent creates bubbles within the softened glass, which in turn creates the foam glass, an inert, non-leaching, rot-resistant, non-flammable, durable construction material." The heating process creates lightweight, porous, gravel-like pieces that weigh far less than standard stone aggregate while still being strong enough to carry heavy loads. Because foam glass is made of closed-cell glass, it is also waterproof. This prevents it from absorbing water and gaining extra weight over the underground structures during heavy rain. The foam glass used along the Arizona highway was made in Florida and transported to the project in large bulk bags. The bags became a noticeable sight for motorists passing the construction area.Promoting sustainability in highway engineeringThe use of foam glass also supports wider sustainability efforts by keeping large amounts of glass waste out of landfills. Glass collected through municipal recycling programmes can be difficult to turn back into new bottles because of sorting problems and mixed colours. Using the material in construction provides another way to reuse it. "Foam glass is not only an innovative material for construction, it's sustainable and environmentally responsible as well," Douglas noted in the publication. The use of foam glass on Interstate 17 is part of a wider trend among US state transport departments looking for lightweight and durable fill materials for soft ground, retaining walls and bridge supports. Similar materials have already been used in European infrastructure, while their use on North American highways has increased as transport agencies consider long-term costs and environmental effects.Progress across the I-17 expansion projectThe I-17 Improvement Project combines traditional construction methods with specialised materials. Along with the foam glass, contractors recycled almost all of the rock removed during major blasting work in the surrounding mountains. The blasted rock was crushed on site and reused for aggregate base, embankment support and paving materials, helping reduce waste. The project has a total investment of about $522 million (£395 million), funded through state highway money, federal infrastructure grants and local regional transport funding. By using lightweight glass aggregate over the existing culverts, construction crews avoided costly structural demolition while keeping the widened road safe and stable for heavy commuter and freight traffic. The completion of the widening work and flex lane installation marks a major step forward for Arizona's transport network.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Egyptian TV presenter sentenced to death on drug charges
articles.summary: Egyptian TV presenter Sarah Khalifa was among 12 people sentenced to death for their alleged role in a drug trafficking network on Saturday, according to a state-owned Egyptian outlet.
articles.body: Egyptian TV presenter Sarah Khalifa was among 12 people sentenced to death for their alleged role in a drug trafficking network on Saturday, according to a state-owned Egyptian outlet. The 12 defendants, including Khalifa, were sentenced to death by hanging and fined 500,000 Egyptian pounds ($9,800) by Cairo’s Criminal Court, the al-Ahram newspaper reported. They were accused of forming an organized criminal gang “specializing in importing substances used in the manufacture of narcotics for the purpose of trafficking,” as well as possessing firearms without a license, al-Ahram said. Nine others were sentenced to life imprisonment and seven were acquitted. Khalifa, who has 2.5 million followers on Instagram, is a well-known presenter who runs her own beauty clinic and hosted an entertainment show with musician Hamo Bika. CNN has contacted her attorney for comment. She wept during the sentencing, asking for “mercy and humanity,” a video circulating on social media appeared to show. CNN was unable to independently verify the footage. “I have never smoked a cigarette in my life,” she could be heard saying. “I swear to Almighty God, with the strongest oath, that I have been wronged.” Prosecutors said the network imported products required for synthetic drug production from abroad, with different individuals responsible for different stages of the process. They said they seized 750 kilograms of synthetic narcotics and other raw materials from a residential property where the defendants allegedly stored and made the drugs. Their case was built on testimony from 20 witnesses, as well as conversations, photographs and video footage, they added. Egypt issued 492 death sentences in 2025, one of the highest recorded rates in the world, according to Amnesty International. The country executed 23 prisoners.

articles.title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
articles.summary: They were transferred onto two lifeboats and taken to shore in the UK.
articles.body:
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.

The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK.

It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel .

The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.

It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.

French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.

Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy .

A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.

"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."

They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

articles.title: In 1974, Michèle Mouton's father gave her an Alpine A110 car with a condition to prove herself or quit; she had entered a man’s world of rallying but 11 years later, she was the ‘fastest woman alive’
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For years, rallying was seen as a man's sport. The cars were brutally fast, the roads unpredictable and the margin for error tiny. Then came Michèle M.
articles.body: For years, rallying was seen as a man's sport. The cars were brutally fast, the roads unpredictable and the margin for error tiny. Then came Michèle Mouton. She did not enter motorsport trying to become the fastest woman. She just wanted to race. At the height of rallying's most dangerous era, Mouton became the first woman to win a round of the World Rally Championship and came within reach of winning the world title.Her story began in Grasse in southern France. Mouton initially worked as a co-driver, accompanying her friend Jean Taibi on the 1972 Tour de Corse. A year later, she moved into the driver's seat. Her father, Pierre, gave her an Alpine A110 with one condition: prove herself during the year or give it up. She proved herself quickly.When male drivers wanted her car checkedMouton's speed was so surprising that some male competitors questioned whether her Alpine was legal. According to the official website of Motor Sport, male drivers pressed the FIA to inspect the car for irregularities. There were none. Mouton also showed that her ability was not limited to rally stages. In 1975, she competed at the 24 Hours of Le Mans as part of an all-female crew and won the 2.0-litre class in a Moynet LM75.But rallying remained her main focus. She moved to a privately entered Porsche 911 in 1977 and earned a factory drive with Fiat France the following year. Her career changed direction when Audi came calling.A car flipped things for herAudi contacted Mouton in 1980, when the company's Quattro was entering competition. “I was called by Audi in 1980, June I think, but I can’t remember who it was,” Mouton recalled in an interview published by Motor Sport. “English was hard for me then, so I went to Ingolstadt with a teacher who could translate.”After a test in Finland with Quattro engineer Walter Treser, Mouton secured a works contract for 1981. The difference between the Audi and the Fiat she had driven was immediately obvious. Mouton later joked that the Fiat 131 felt “like a truck” compared with the Quattro.The Audi had more power and power steering, but it also required Mouton to understand a very different machine. “I didn’t like technical things so much, so I had to learn and adapt and understand how it worked,” she said.She would soon show exactly what she could do with it.1981: The win that changed women's place in the WRCMouton began the 1981 World Rally Championship season with co-driver Fabrizia Pons. Audi knew an all-female crew had publicity value, but few expected Mouton to challenge the established stars immediately. The Quattro itself had reliability problems, while Audi was still building its rally operation.Mouton nevertheless finished eighth overall in the championship. Then came the Sanremo Rally. Mouton and Pons won outright, making Mouton the first woman to win a round of the World Rally Championship.It remains the defining achievement of her WRC career. The following season, she went even further.Three wins and a world title within reachThe 1982 season began badly after a crash at Monte Carlo. But Mouton responded by winning in Portugal, Greece and Brazil. The Portugal victory came in difficult conditions, with spectators crowding sections of the route and dense fog making the stages even harder. By the penultimate round, the Côte d'Ivoire Rally, Mouton was fighting Walter Röhrl for the world championship. The rally was an exceptionally demanding event, covering around 750 miles of gravel.Then, just before the start, Mouton received devastating news. Her father had died of cancer. “My father died at 7 a.m., and the race started at 8:30 a.m.,” she recalled. “I wanted to go home but my mother said to drive.” Only Pons knew what had happened. Mouton started the rally. She built a lead of 1 hour and 20 minutes over Röhrl before a gearbox change cost her 1 hour and 15 minutes. More problems followed. She pushed to recover the lost time but eventually crashed out.The championship went to Röhrl. Mouton finished second overall in the 1982 World Rally Championship, still the best WRC championship result achieved by a woman. Her reaction was not about the title. “I lost the world championship, but I missed my father more,” she said.Her second-place finish in Rally GB also helped Audi secure the manufacturers' championship, the first such title for an all-wheel-drive car.Then she went up Pikes PeakMouton's WRC opportunities were reduced after 1983. She finished fifth in the 1983 championship, while Audi teammate Hannu Mikkola won the title. Audi later signed Röhrl, leaving Mouton with only limited opportunities. But Audi of America gave her another challenge: the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb in Colorado.The 12-mile climb was run over dirt and gravel, with hundreds of corners and steep drops. Mouton competed there in 1984, winning her class despite engine problems and the added weight of carrying co-driver Pons. In 1985, she returned alone. And won outright. Mouton completed the climb in 11 minutes 25.39 seconds, beating established American names including Bobby Unser. She also broke the overall course record, set by Al Unser, by 13 seconds.But the race was not without controversy. Mouton said officials had made things difficult after she exceeded a low speed limit during practice by a small amount. She was ordered to pay a fine, and officials wanted her to run to the car before the start, in the style of an old Le Mans start.Mouton publicly argued that the arrangement was dangerous because it could encourage a driver to enter the car and begin driving without properly securing the seatbelt. She was eventually required to start with the car out of gear. She won anyway. “They didn’t know how determined I am!” she later said.When the cars became almost impossible to tameMouton drove several versions of Audi's Quattro, including the increasingly powerful Group B cars. Of them, she preferred the first short-wheelbase Quattro, particularly its twin-clutch PDK gearbox. But she also recognised how quickly the cars were becoming difficult to control.She said the later short-wheelbase car had about 530 bhp on asphalt and had become so fast that finding the limit left drivers with very little time to react. “Gravel always showed you the limit. You could feel it,” she explained.Group B would eventually become infamous for the dangers surrounding it. Lancia driver Attilio Bettega was killed on Corsica in 1985. In 1986, a Ford RS200 crashed into spectators during the Portugal Rally, killing people. Then came the accident that would end the era. During the 1986 Tour de Corse, Mouton was driving a Peugeot 205 T16. She had retired two stages before Henri Toivonen and co-driver Sergio Cresto were killed when their car crashed and caught fire. Mouton and Toivonen were friends.“I had retired two stages before the accident, so I was in the service park when we heard. It was terrible. Terrible,” she recalled. The deaths ultimately contributed to the end of Group B.She left rallying but did not leave motorsportMouton won the 1986 German Rally Championship and continued competing in rally raids with Peugeot until 1989. She then retired from competition and turned to raising her family. Her daughter was born in 1987. But motorsport remained part of her life. In 1988, Mouton helped establish the Race of Champions, initially created as a contest between WRC champions in identical cars. The event later became a meeting point for drivers from different motorsport disciplines.Mouton's work in motorsport also moved beyond competition. From 2010 until her retirement in 2022, she served as president of the FIA Women in Motorsport Commission, which promotes women's participation across motorsport. Her career was also the subject of the Emmy-winning documentary “Queen of Speed” in 2021.Mouton's career is often described through the fact that she was a woman competing in a male-dominated sport. That is an important part of the story, but it was never how she measured herself. She won when the cars were difficult to control, competed against drivers who had no reason to make space for her and came within one rally of becoming the first woman to win the World Rally Championship.No woman has finished higher than Mouton's second place in the WRC championship. By the end of her career, the question was no longer whether a woman could compete. It was whether anyone could keep up with Michèle Mouton.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: German far-right set for big win in eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt - projections
articles.summary: Germany's AfD has hailed a "historic result" and is projected to win more than 44% of the vote, far ahead of the conservative CDU on 18.4%.
articles.body:
Germany's AfD is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, according to initial projections. It is not yet clear if that would be enough to take power in the state but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.

The far-right party is set to win more than 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on 18.2%.

The AfD has hailed the result as a "historic outcome" and its charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, has refused to govern with any other party.

No far-right party has won control of a state in Germany since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.

Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund.

The AfD's projected result is higher than earlier opinion polls suggested, and Siegmund along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as the news emerged.

However, party leaders will not know if they have enough seats to govern until they see which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament.

That may hinge on whether one of the smaller parties gets over the required threshold of 5%.

If the populist left-wing BSW fails to get in, then the AfD's chances of a majority increase. The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament.

A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.

A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem.

"We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory and said his party would have to deal with the result: "This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign."

Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin".

AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland . It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result as well. Although the outcome was initially unclear, the party's supporters believe they are on the march.

Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at an estimated 78%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters.

One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give."

"No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC.

Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.

The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.

They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

articles.title: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks
articles.summary: The comments came a day after Washington said it had struck Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran's attacks on US warships in the region.
articles.body:
Iran's top negotiator has warned of "a faster, heavier, and more painful response" to US attacks, as hostilities between the two sides escalate.

Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday that Americans must understand "before it is too late" that the "rules of the game have changed", according to a translation of his comments on state media.

His comments come nearly a week into renewed fighting between Iran and the US, and a day after Washington said it struck Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran attacking American warships in the region's waters.

The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom) for comment.

Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz.

"The report came from Iranian state media and it's a total lie," said Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, according to the Associated Press.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued his own threats back at Iran, writing on social media on Saturday, "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."

A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, and that period of relative calm was shattered when the US resumed attacks last Sunday.

Fighting has continued throughout the week, with the US launching multiple strikes on Iranian targets and Iran retaliating against US targets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.

US President Donald Trump said this week that the renewed fighting would not last "too long", echoing comments both he and his administration have frequently made since the now six-month-long war began in February.

Months of negotiations between the US and Iran have not amounted to lasting peace, and there's little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon.

The Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to the world's oil and gas industry, has been effectively closed since the war began, and has become a major source of leverage for Iran.

Tehran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway.

But Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.

The conflict in the strait has led to an increase in gas prices globally, and ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers.

The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US hit $5.85 on Friday, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that an average of 9 million barrels of oil a day were passing through the strait, which could help ease pressure on energy prices.

Wright told CNN with oil also moving through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows".

In an interview with ABC This Week on Sunday, Wright added that gas prices should start to come down for Americans as summer demand begins to wane after Labor Day.

articles.title: China’s ‘chemical trap’ targets hidden nuclear fuel in seawater, beats US benchmark 8 times over
articles.summary: China News: Chinese researchers have developed a new material capable of extracting uranium from seawater at more than eight times the target rate previously set .
articles.body: Chinese researchers have developed a new material capable of extracting uranium from seawater at more than eight times the target rate previously set by the US department of energy, SCMP reported. This marks a potential advancement in the global effort to tap the oceans as a vast source of nuclear fuel.The team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Qingdao recovered up to 50.4mg of uranium per gram of the material from natural seawater samples, compared with the US benchmark of 6mg per gram.The material, known as PhosCage, is a sponge-like molecular structure containing phosphate groups that chemically bind uranium. Researchers later converted it into millimetre-sized beads that could be easier to deploy and retrieve outside laboratory settings.The beads extracted 22.55mg of uranium per gram of material and remained effective through seven cycles of reuse, according to the researchers.“This work opens up a novel approach to extracting uranium from seawater and lays the groundwork for adsorbents that can capture more uranium and eventually be used on a large scale,” the team from the CAS’ Qingdao Institute of Bioenergy and Bioprocess Technology said in a statement.Why seawater uranium mattersThe technology could have particular significance for China as its nuclear power programme expands faster than domestic uranium production.China produced about 1,600 tonnes of uranium from domestic mines in 2024, while its nuclear reactors required roughly 13,000 tonnes, according to the World Nuclear Association. The gap has left the country heavily dependent on imports.Seawater offers a potentially enormous alternative resource.The world has about 7.9 million tonnes of known uranium resources on land, while the oceans are estimated to contain around 4.5 billion tonnes. Uranium has accumulated in seawater over geological time after being washed from rocks by rain and carried into the oceans through rivers.The scale of the resource is vast, but extracting it remains extremely challenging.A tonne of seawater contains only about 3.3mg of uranium, meaning enormous quantities of water would have to be processed to recover significant amounts of the metal.The problem with finding uraniumUranium is also surrounded by a range of other dissolved elements in seawater, creating a major separation challenge.Vanadium is particularly problematic because it can bind to the same chemical sites used to capture uranium, making it difficult to isolate the desired element.Researchers in the US have spent years attempting to overcome these challenges. Oak Ridge National Laboratory developed specialised fibres designed to capture uranium, while Pacific Northwest National Laboratory tested the technology using naturally flowing seawater from Washington's Sequim Bay.By 2016, the best US adsorbents were recovering about 6mg of uranium per gram after prolonged exposure to seawater. However, the approach remained considerably more expensive than conventional uranium mining, and the US Department of Energy largely withdrew from the programme after it ended in 2018.China material shows uranium preferenceThe Qingdao researchers say their work addresses some of the key technical hurdles involved in uranium extraction.Two studies published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials and Separation and Purification Technology found that the bead-based material displayed a strong preference for uranium when exposed to multiple metals.Importantly, it was able to preferentially capture uranium over vanadium, one of the elements that has traditionally made seawater extraction particularly difficult.However, the results remain at the laboratory stage. The researchers collected seawater from the coast of Qingdao and processed 25 litres through a laboratory flow system. The material was not tested in the open ocean, where waves, currents, marine organisms and changing environmental conditions could complicate the extraction process.Neither study established the cost of producing the recovered uranium.The researchers said further work would focus on scaling up the material and reducing the overall cost of extracting uranium from seawater.For China, success on those fronts could potentially provide another source of nuclear fuel and reduce some of its dependence on imported uranium. For the wider nuclear industry, the research represents another step in the long-running effort to turn the oceans' enormous uranium reserves into a commercially viable resource.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers
articles.summary: Tehran says time for proportionate retaliation is over after a US strike on Iranian tankers inside the blockade line.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – The United States continues to rely on a mix of military force and economic sanctions against Iran, which has so far only prompted authorities in Tehran to consider more forceful responses.

The US Central Command (CENTCOM) released video on Saturday showing three Iranian crude oil tankers being hit – one off Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, another near Jask and a third in the Gulf of Oman. Two were “permanently disabled”, while a third sank after extensive bombing, CENTCOM said.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later aired video of its own, showing explosives-laden projectiles crashing into multiple ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Aggressor US must know that it has no way but to leave the region and stop its malignance,” the IRGC said in a statement on Sunday. It added that a US-built sea drone was hit while trying to enter Iranian waters in the vital waterway, through which one fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.

The IRGC also said on Sunday it had fired several ballistic missiles towards a US aircraft carrier and another warship that are part of the network of vessels imposing the months-long naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports. Both vessels sustained some damage and fled, said the IRGC, although there was no immediate evidence of a successful hit and CENTCOM said the attacks were “evaded”.

The IRGC said it considered the acknowledgement by the US that missiles were launched towards its warships as “live evidence of the enemy’s strategic defeat and proof” of the force’s “offensive capabilities”.

Speaking during a private meeting of parliament members on Sunday, Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tehran has inflicted “significant blows” to US bases across the region to the “frustration” of leaders in Washington.

“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases was only a start,” said Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s chief negotiator with the US.

Any further attacks against Iranian interests will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” strikes from Iran, he warned.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the US attacks on Iranian ships illegal and a “war crime” that runs counter to the United Nations Charter.

US and Iranian officials provide different readings of what is transpiring after months of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the naval blockade imposed since mid-July.

The administration of President Donald Trump says more vessels have transited the strategically important waterway over recent weeks under US guidance, despite threats and attacks from Iran, with traffic allegedly nearing pre-war levels on some days. That account is countered by Iranian authorities, which say the strait remains closed.

The US military said about 90 commercial vessels have been redirected as part of the blockade, with several more disabled or boarded.

Crude oil exports from the Middle East during August were down 39 percent since the January and February baseline of 18.5 million barrels per day (mbpd), according to TankerTrackers. It said the current deficit is now 7.2mbpd, down from 12.4mbpd in May.

“Although most may recover in the coming months, Iran’s exports of 1.68mbpd (baseline number) may likely remain at zero for the foreseeable future; depending on any agreement,” the maritime intelligence company posted online on Sunday.

Iranian authorities have confirmed that they have been unable to get crude oil past the US warships imposing the blockade.

But they pointed out it does not equal a total halt to exports, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying late last month that up to 90 million barrels of oil were exported during the brief period that the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June was in effect.

Some of the oil is kept in floating storage outside the blockade, allowing Iran to gradually sell it at a discount to its main oil customer, China, despite US sanctions.

Washington is counting on those supplies running out in the foreseeable future.

“There’s probably only about 30 million barrels of Iranian crude oil left that China hasn’t bought,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday. “So that will run out soon and there will be no problem with China buying because they have no product.”

Bessent again hailed the “one-two punch” of the blockade and sanctions as part of what the Trump administration has branded Operation Economic Outcast , aimed at reducing Iran’s trade with neighbours and further isolating 90 million Iranians.

Iranian authorities have not said how much longer they expect to be able to sell oil amid the US onslaught, nor have they elaborated on whether they are exploring potential alternative routes.

But experts have said that while overland and rail routes can move limited refined products, fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas towards Afghanistan, Iraq, Central Asia and beyond, they cannot offer a viable and scalable replacement for the volume transported by very large crude carriers through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Economy Ministry on Sunday established an “economic war headquarters” to counter the pressure , as the country deals with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, unemployment, energy imbalance and a host of other deep-seated issues.

But IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi suggested that the US was taking several times more economic damage from the war and blockade than Iran.

“If the US wants to deal one dollar in economic damage to Iran, it may deal several dollars’ worth of costs and damages to itself,” he said, pointing to lowered US strategic energy reserves and decreased aluminium exports from the region as examples.

articles.title: Hurricane Marie to impact California coast with dangerous surf, coastal flooding over Labour Day weekend
articles.summary: US News: Hurricane Marie is bringing powerful swells, dangerous rip currents, and coastal flooding to Southern California, with beaches from Los Angeles to Ora.
articles.body: Hurricane Marie is bringing powerful swells, dangerous rip currents, and coastal flooding to Southern California, with beaches from Los Angeles to Orange County experiencing hazardous conditions over the Labour Day weekend.While the hurricane is expected to remain well offshore and is not forecast to make landfall in California, its powerful swells have already caused flooding and prompted water rescues along the coast.The storm, which strengthened to a Category 2 hurricane over the eastern Pacific, is churning off the coast of Baja California.The National Weather Service (NWS) has warned of large breaking waves, strong rip currents, beach erosion and coastal flooding across parts of Southern California through Tuesday.At Seal Beach on Saturday, seawater surged into parking lots near the pier, flooding low-lying areas and trapping vehicles, according to US media reports.Video obtained by ABC7 showed around a dozen people working together to push a vehicle out of the floodwaters.Crews later built a berm and pumped seawater back toward the ocean as wet sand spread across the boardwalk and flooding remained visible near some shoreline homes. The 8th Street and 10th Street parking lots were expected to remain closed through Wednesday.The hazardous surf also prompted a lifeguard rescue in Manhattan Beach, where large swells and strong currents created dangerous conditions despite Marie remaining hundreds of miles offshore.Los Angeles County lifeguards are preparing for a particularly busy holiday weekend, with officials expecting more than 1,000 water rescues. Typical daily rescues number around 500."We're expecting to see these elevated wave heights in the 3- to 5-foot range, with sets up to 6- to 8-feet" at some beaches, including Zuma Beach and Malibu, Los Angeles County Fire Department ocean lifeguard specialist Jake Miller told ABC7.The NWS has warned of an increased risk of drowning, saying rip currents could become widespread and very strong. Large waves could also sweep people from rocks and beaches, injure beachgoers and overturn small boats close to shore.Low-lying coastal areas around Avalon, Long Beach's Alamitos Peninsula and the coastline from Oxnard to Malibu, including Point Mugu, are particularly vulnerable to seawater flooding around high tide, the NWS said.In San Diego County, forecasters have also warned of dangerous surf, with breaking waves potentially reaching 6 to 10 feet along parts of the coastline. High tides could worsen flooding in vulnerable coastal areas.Despite the storm's impact on coastal conditions, Marie is not expected to make landfall in California. The National Hurricane Center expects the system to weaken and become a post-tropical remnant low by Wednesday.However, its swells are expected to continue affecting Southern California beaches for several days, keeping the risk of dangerous surf and rip currents elevated.Authorities have requested beachgoers to check conditions before entering the water, avoid areas with strong currents and stay away from rocks and exposed coastal areas.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Missouri foster mom accused of trading teen for monkey avoids prison
articles.summary: Brenda Deutsch received a suspended sentence after allegedly trading a foster teen for a monkey, as the judge called her actions reprehensible.
articles.body: A Missouri foster mother accused of trading a teenage girl for a monkey avoided prison time, even as a judge condemned her as reprehensible and apologized to her alleged victims for a foster care system he said had failed them. Brenda Deutsch, 70, was sentenced to seven years in prison for child endangerment, but a Lincoln County judge suspended execution of the sentence and placed her on three years of probation, allowing her to remain free if she complies with its terms, FOX2 St. Louis reported. Judge Thomas Frawley also revoked Deutsch’s foster care license from the bench and criticized the state of Missouri for allowing her to keep it. FLORIDA COUPLE ALLEGEDLY HELD FOUR CHILDREN IN TRACTOR-TRAILER CAB FOR NEARLY SIX YEARS Frawley then apologized to the victims in the courtroom, telling them he was sorry the system had failed them. Deutsch’s biological daughter, Brina Johnson, who testified about alleged abuse, said the outcome was not what she had hoped for. "I’m kinda lost for words because this is not the end we wished for," Johnson told FOX2. Johnson said a teenager present in the courtroom was the foster child at the center of allegations that Deutsch traded her for a monkey. "I have the whole conversation on my phone, which I turned over to the detectives," Johnson said. "That’s what she did; she had at least seven monkeys," Johnson said. "That’s just her thing. But she wasn’t any nicer to those monkeys than she was to a child." Deutsch was arrested in April after authorities investigated allegations that she sent the foster child, who is now 17, to Texas to stay in a home Deutsch admitted in court she knew nothing about. Court documents previously obtained by Fox News Digital said the investigation began after Deutsch sought permission to take the girl to visit a friend in Texas. Five days later, an anonymous caller alerted the Missouri Department of Social Services Children’s Division that Deutsch was allegedly physically and mentally abusing the child. Investigators later learned of an allegation that the girl had been traded for an exotic animal and was living in Texas. 69 LIVE ANIMALS FOUND STUFFED IN PILLOWCASES IN HIDDEN CAR COMPARTMENT AFTER BORDER ARREST: FEDS The teenager told investigators Deutsch informed her Texas friend that the friend could keep the child, but Deutsch "will be keeping the check," according to court documents. A witness told police the girl had been left in an unsanitary Texas home filled with exotic animals. She was eventually taken into the custody of child protective services in Texas. The teenager also described alleged abuse by Deutsch, telling investigators she was struck with objects including a paddle and shoes. During one alleged beating, she said she lay on the floor and tried to "soften the strikes to her body," according to court documents. Deutsch also allegedly took away the girl’s clothes and once threatened to kill her "if she did not shut up," the documents said. Deutsch declined to comment outside the courthouse, shielding her face with a piece of paper as she walked to her vehicle and drove away. Deutsch has reportedly fostered more than 200 children over the years. Johnson said the judge’s acknowledgment of the system’s failures offered some validation despite her disappointment with the outcome. And the system did fail us, failed them all." Fox News Digital's Julia Bonavita contributed to this report.

articles.title: Andrew Williams, Every Time I Die guitarist known as ‘The Butcher’ to wrestling fans, dies
articles.summary: Andrew Williams, the longtime rhythm guitarist for metalcore band Every Time I Die, who went by “The Butcher” in his other career as a professional wrestler, has died, All Elite Wrestling has confirmed.
articles.body: Andrew Williams, the longtime rhythm guitarist for metalcore band Every Time I Die, who went by “The Butcher” in his other career as a professional wrestler, has died, All Elite Wrestling has confirmed. He was 48. Williams’ death was announced hours after he collapsed during an independent wrestling show in Millvale, Pennsylvania, and was rushed to a hospital by ambulance Saturday night. “Andy collapsed at the end of his match this evening,” Enjoy Wrestling, the promoter putting on Saturday’s event, said on X. “Our doctors on staff tended to him immediately, administering CPR until the ambulance arrived.” Williams grew up in the Buffalo, New York, area, thinking he was going to follow his father’s and uncles’ footsteps and work at a factory when he got older. “I remember being like, ‘Oh, my God, I got to get out of here,’” he told Renee Paquette in a 2022 interview. Williams recalled living with learning disabilities, including dyslexia, which prevented him from learning how to read music. But, he told Paquette, “I just picked up a guitar and it just made sense.” Williams played with Every Time I Die from the group’s inception in 1998 to it’s disbandment in 2022. “The band became known for turning chaos into catharsis, pairing breakneck intensity with anthemic hooks and off-kilter grooves,” according to Epitaph Records, which signed the group in 2008. In 2025, Williams’ new band, Atomic Rule, released a demo EP. On Saturday, just hours before his collapse, Williams spoke in a video on the group’s Instagram page, saying they’d just wrapped up writing new music and would be appearing on tour with Gwar in November and December. “Get ready, because Atomic Rule is going to be coming and smashing it,” Williams said in the video. Between the ropes, Williams dispensed with his soft-spoken, easygoing demeanor and instead went by “The Butcher,” putting his burly, heavily tattooed body to hard-hitting use as one half of the tag team “The Butcher and The Blade.” Though he’d loved pro wrestling as a child, he told the “HardLore” podcast in 2025 that it wasn’t until he attended a show held by Southern California indie promotion Pro Wrestling Guerrilla around 2014 that the idea of becoming a wrestler himself finally crystalized in his mind. In 2015, at age 37, he finally wrestled his first full match. Four years later, he’d debut on All Elite Wrestling, performing on television until his contract expired in 2026. Williams described the similarities between music and wrestling to “HardLore.” “Anyone who’s written a song can wrestle a wrestling match,” he said. “It’s very similar to like — putting a song together is just like putting a wrestling match together. There’s ups and downs, there’s peaks and valleys.” Despite his talents in two different arenas, Williams told interviewer and wrestling personality Alicia Atout in a 2017 interview that his “true life calling is just to make my friends laugh.” “That makes me feel like a million bucks, if I can get dudes rolling,” he said. Former colleagues and fans began paying tribute to Williams on Sunday. Josh Eppard, the drummer for rock band Coheed and Cambria, called Williams’ death “beyond heartbreaking” and recalled his kindness, saying he met Williams during a 2019 tour. “Peace to Andy, the kind giant who I thought was doing some backyard wrestling s--- with his buddies until one day I saw his mug on the TV and was in stunned disbelief,” Eppard said. “Andy was not only a pillar of one of the most true and influential bands in heavy music, he was also pulling double duty as a pro wrestler????” Wrestler Matt Hardy, who worked with Williams at AEW, called him a “kind, funny & deep individual who was an extremely talented musician & wrestler.” RJ City, an AEW interviewer and member of the company’s creative team, highlighted Williams’ intellect. “Andy Williams was so smart and cultured that it made both his chosen careers all the more insane,” City said. “He was the opposite of how he looked, we were lucky to know him.” Former AEW women’s world champion Willow Nightingale recalled Williams encouraging her, raising her confidence and advocating for her before she’d been signed to the company. “He had every right to have an ego, but he didn’t,” Nightingale said. “He reached his hand out and did what he could to help others.” Wrestler Josh Alexander called Williams “one of the best people I ever met.” “I’ll remember Andy for what he was,” Alexander wrote on X. “A dude with an enormous heart that could always put a smile on my face.”

articles.title: Erica Baker missing since February 7, 1999, in Kettering, Ohio | Dateline
articles.summary: 9-year-old Erica Baker has been missing since February 7, 1999, in Kettering, Ohio. The Kettering Police Department is investigating.
articles.body: Sunday, Feb. 7, 1999. A rainy day in Kettering, Ohio. Nine-year-old Erica Baker was looking forward to a special event with her dad. “We were supposed to go to the father-daughter dance at the rec center,” Greg Baker told “Dateline.” Greg, who shared custody with Erica’s mother, said it was his day with his daughter. “I was unable to obtain tickets which -- she was a little upset over that,” he recalled. So Greg dropped his daughter back at her mother’s house earlier than usual. Around 6 p.m., his phone rang. “I get a phone call from her mother saying they can’t find Erica,” he said. His daughter was missing. Erica grew up in Kettering, a southwestern Ohio town Greg describes as “suburban, laid-back” and safe. She enjoyed spending time in the neighborhood with friends, but most of all, she loved keeping up with her three older brothers. “She was a combination of a tomboy and a princess,” Greg said. “I raised her up to be able to fish and camp and do all the things that a little boy would do.” By 1999, Greg and Erica’s mother, Misty, were no longer together. Greg said he had the kids on weekends and during the summers. The weekend of Feb. 7 was Greg’s turn with the children. He had hoped to take Erica to the father-daughter dance, but the tickets were sold out. Greg believes that disappointment may have been one reason Erica wanted to go home early. So that afternoon, he dropped Erica and her three brothers back at Misty’s house. “I told her that I loved her, and I would see her next week,” Greg remembered. He said he headed back to his home in Huber Heights, about 15 minutes away. Around 6 p.m., Greg got a call from Misty. Erica was nowhere to be found. “So I immediately started panicking, and I came from Huber Heights and made it there pretty fast, running a lot of red lights, unfortunately, to get there,” he said. Greg says Kettering police were already at the scene when he arrived. “They were letting me know that she had not returned home,” he said. Bob Green, now retired, was the first detective assigned to Erica’s case. “I was called out that night,” Green told “Dateline.” “I had only been a detective for about four or five months.” Green says that around 4 p.m. on Feb. 7, an older couple walking their dog near a pond by Kettering Middle School and the recreation center encountered a little girl who was also walking a dog. “Erica was walking away from the pond with her dog, and the two dogs kind of interacted, barking,” Green recalled the couple saying. The couple continued their walk, according to Green. As they were leaving, the couple spotted Erica’s dog, Jamie, alone near the middle school. “They then retrieved the dog and took the dog to the rec center and called the police,” Green said. At that point, Green said, police thought they were simply dealing with a lost dog. But at Erica’s home, the family was already starting to worry that Erica hadn’t come home. “Around 5 p.m., the family started searching for Erica because it was getting dark and she was afraid of the dark,” Green said. “They searched a lot.” Eventually, the family called the police. Once officers connected the missing girl with the dog that had been found near the recreation center, a massive law enforcement search began. “We had horses, ATVs, canines, people on foot,” Green told “Dateline.” “I think we might have had the helicopter. Just a ton of searching.” Greg Baker told “Dateline” much of the search centered around the rec center, where Erica had last been seen walking. He thinks she may have gone there because that’s where the father-daughter dance she’d hoped to attend was being held. “They called search teams in and were asking for volunteers that showed up at the rec center,” Greg said. Divers also searched the nearby pond where the couple said they had run into Erica. Investigators feared she may have slipped and drowned, a theory Greg doubted. “Erica was always very knowledgeable because, number one, we did a lot of fishing, a lot of swimming, a lot of camping,” he said. “She knows that those are dangerous places that you shouldn’t be.” According to Greg, investigators eventually drained the pond. “Of course, they didn’t find anything,” he said. Early on, investigators and the family believed Erica had been abducted. “It was out of her normal behavior to run away,” retired detective Green said. Investigators began looking closely at the people in Erica’s life, starting with her parents. Greg says he and Misty had the spotlight on them from the start, which is to be expected. “When it comes to disappearing children and stuff, the parents are pretty much the focal point at that point in time, especially when parents are divorced,” he explained. “They kind of were looking at me and Misty pretty hot and heavy.” According to Greg, he and Misty each took a polygraph test, which he says they passed. Green told “Dateline” he ruled out both of Erica’s parents as being involved pretty early on. Police continued following tips and leads. Then, four months after Erica’s disappearance, the investigation headed in a different direction. In June 1999, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) sent two retired officers to Kettering to review the investigation with fresh eyes. “They took a day or two and just went through all this stuff,” Green recalled. “And then they gave us suggestions.” One of those suggestions was to interview Clifford Butts, an inmate at an Ohio prison. “And he’s the one who told us about Christian Gabriel,” Green said. According to Green, Christian Gabriel had struggled with drugs and been in and out of prison. During a previous stint in the Dayton jail, he met Clifford Butts. “They became friends somewhere in that time,” Green said. According to Green, Butts told investigators that on Feb. 7, 1999 — the day Erica disappeared — he and his wife met up with Gabriel and his girlfriend at the time, Jan Franks. Butts told investigators that later that day, he and Gabriel sat together in Gabriel’s van. “And that’s when Christian says he hit a little girl and they had to get rid of her body,” Green said. Green says Butts told investigators that the next day, he and Gabriel came across a missing person flyer with Erica’s picture on it. “And Christian told Clifford, ‘You see that girl? That’s the girl I hit,’” Green said. According to Green, shortly after speaking with Butts in June 1999, investigators located Gabriel’s van at a tow yard. They obtained a warrant and sent it to a crime lab to be searched, but the examination yielded no evidence. Green told “Dateline” that investigators then brought in Christian Gabriel and Jan Franks for questioning. Both denied having anything to do with Erica’s disappearance. According to Green, investigators administered polygraph tests to the couple, and the results for both indicated deception. However, he noted, there was not enough evidence to bring charges in connection to Erica’s case at the time. Jan Franks died in 2001. Investigators kept their eyes on Gabriel. In mid-2004, while Gabriel was serving time for an unrelated theft case, Green questioned him again. “He lies. Or I find something new and I want to go visit him and talk to him — and he lies,” Green said. But in December 2004, Green got what he called “half a confession.” According to Green, while Gabriel was still incarcerated on the theft case, Green asked to speak with him again. Green says this time, Gabriel told him that he and Jan had been stealing from stores on the afternoon of Feb. 7, 1999. Green says Gabriel told him he and Jan were driving when they spotted a Kettering police cruiser at a local grocery store. They thought the officers might be looking for them, so they took off, eventually ending up near the Kettering Recreation Center. “And he says this little girl darted out in front of him, and he hit her,” Green recalled. According to Green, Gabriel said he picked Erica up, put her in the van, and attempted CPR. Gabriel claimed he wanted to take Erica to a hospital, but said Jan refused because she was wanted by authorities. “So then they drove off, and they disposed of her body,” Green said. In a witness statement filed with the Kettering Police Department at the time, Gabriel wrote that he and Jan Franks were driving in his van on Feb. 7, 1999, when they struck Erica with the vehicle. He went on to say that he wanted to take Erica to the hospital, but Jan refused because she was afraid they would get into trouble. Instead, he wrote, they “carried her into the woods dug a whole and buried her.” In the statement, dated December 2004, Gabriel apologized to the family “for what had been an accident that turned out really bad.” Green says Gabriel later showed investigators the road near the recreation center where he said Erica had been hit. “It was the first time in five years that we had a crime scene.” Green told “Dateline” Gabriel did not lead them to Erica’s body. He believes Gabriel may have withheld the location because finding Erica’s remains could reveal more about how she died — and potentially expose him to more serious charges. “If we were to find her and prove that she was murdered, then we’re not talking vehicular homicide anymore,” Green said. “We’re talking murder.” On Feb. 7, 2005, the sixth anniversary of Erica’s disappearance, a grand jury indicted Gabriel on charges of gross abuse of a corpse and tampering with evidence. He was convicted and served six years in prison. He was not indicted on any murder charges. Gabriel appealed his convictions in 2007, arguing that police had pressured him into making statements and that there hadn’t been enough evidence to support the charges. He also challenged the trial court’s handling of other issues in the case, including his sentence. The Ohio Court of Appeals upheld his convictions. In 2023, Kettering Police Detective Amy Pedro took over Erica’s case. She says Green was released in 2011 and later left Ohio. Pedro, a violent crimes detective, grew up in Kettering just blocks from where Erica disappeared. Her father was also a Kettering police officer and worked on Erica’s case in 1999. When Pedro inherited the case, she says she went back through nearly three decades of reports and tips. “My job was just to read all the reports and get to know the case as well as possible,” she told “Dateline.” Pedro says the investigation remains active. “It’s definitely open. It’s very open. It’s very active,” she said. “And we continue to do searches.” While investigators currently have no physical evidence, they do have family DNA standards on file, which Pedro says could help identify Erica if her remains are ever recovered. Pedro believes Gabriel remains the person most likely to tell investigators what happened to Erica — and where she may be. “Our one suspect is the only one that will be able to tell us where Erica is in the long run,” she said. “I need Christian Gabriel to have a coming to Jesus with himself and understand that this little girl needs to be put to rest with her family, and this family needs to find some peace out of this case.” Green also strongly believes Gabriel can lead them to where Erica’s body is buried. “Christian Gabriel killed her. And he told me he killed her,” Green said. “Dateline” reached out to Christian Gabriel for comment but did not receive a response. Related: “Dateline” learned about Erica’s case while working on the episode “No Ordinary Sunday” for Season 5 of the Dateline: Missing in America podcast series. Niqui McCown disappeared from nearby Richmond, Indiana, in July 2001. For Greg Baker, nearly three decades of searching have not brought the answer he wants most — where his daughter is. “It takes a toll on people,” he told “Dateline.” “I’m surprised that I can get up in the morning and put my shoes on.” He wishes he could have had that last dance with his daughter. “I’ve had nightmares over this throughout the years — and with the father-daughter dance and me not able to get tickets,” Greg said. “I mean, I have grieved over that situation for many years.” But more than anything, Greg just wants Erica found and brought home. He’s not the only one. “I would like for her to be recovered so they have a headstone at a cemetery in Kettering,” retired detective Bob Green told Dateline. “And I would hope that we would be able to recover her remains for them so they have a place to visit and they can get closure, whatever that is for them.” At the time of her disappearance, Erica was 3’11” and weighed 65 lbs. She was last seen wearing a Winnie-the-Pooh shirt, a pink raincoat, and white tennis shoes. She would be 37 years old today. Anyone with information about Erica Baker’s disappearance is asked to contact the Kettering Police Department at 937-296-2460.

articles.title: Palestinian farmers battle settler sabotage to save Hebron crops, livestock
articles.summary: West Bank farmers defy daily settler attacks, sheep theft, and military restrictions to protect their land.
articles.body:
Amid the grapevines that once provided a steady income for her family, 56-year-old Palestinian farmer Theeba al-Sabaa spends much of her day guarding her home and farmland in the occupied West Bank from settlers.

From dusk till dawn, she works on her land in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, known by locals as “Jabal Sabaa”.

Theeba is engaged in a daily battle against the encroaching settler outposts that have emerged among the rolling hills that surround her, and which block access to sections of her land.

“By God, the land has taught me patience, and to cling to my right, for as long as I have a right, I must take it and never let it go,” she told Al Jazeera.

“I will never leave it because I worked hard on it, I toil and sweat on it, so I will not leave my toil and sweat, or the toil of my children and my husband, to go to someone else.”

Since mid-2024, when settlers established new outposts on the nearby hills, every one of Theeba’s moves has been monitored.

Settlers frequently approach the perimeter of her home and deliberately release livestock into the cultivated fields.

“They enter with their sheep into our land after we plow and fix it, grazing in it, trampling the crops, and stomping on them with their sheep, leaving nothing,” Theeba said.

“As soon as they feel any movement or anyone entering the land, you find them attacking us immediately.”

This intimidation extends to the adjacent fields, where 59-year-old Anwar Sabarneh lives with his extended family of seven brothers.

Due to the repeated settler violations, two of his brothers have been forced to abandon their land.

Sabarneh, who supports a family of 14, owns several dunams of vineyards located just 300 metres (980 feet) from his home. With aggressive settlers around, reaching them has become a dangerous ordeal.

Sabarneh said that the Israeli army even demands permits from Palestinians to work on their own land.

“The army came with the settlers to ask me for a permit so I can work in my home, in front of my house’s door, and on my land where I am the rightful owner,” Sabarneh said.

Farmers are also barred from building anything on their land. Sabarneh’s sheep have also been locked in a barn for over eight months due to the dangers posed by settlers.

“If they see me taking the sheep out, the settlers chase me, kidnap them, and steal them,” he said.

When Sabarneh’s children have tried to retrieve their stolen sheep, Israeli soldiers have arrested and beaten them.

Repeated pogroms by settlers against Palestinian farmers reflect a broader strategy targeting agriculture across the southern West Bank.

Settlers and the Israeli troops carried out 11,074 attacks in the West Bank during the first half of 2026, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission. This includes 3,488 carried out by settlers.

Hasan Breijieh, a settlement affairs expert and director at the commission, told Al Jazeera that continuous settlement expansionism, alongside restrictions on Palestinian movement, are the primary reasons that so many Palestinians have been forced to flee their farms.

“Military gates erected at the entrances of Palestinian communities have tightened control over… access to their orchards and vineyards,” he said.

Bypass roads, built by Israel, have also hindered “connectivity between Palestinian communities”, Breijieh said.

Under such restrictions, Palestinian farmers have faced a fourth consecutive season without being able to harvest olives, grapes, or guava. Their lands have been “neither plowed nor pruned”, and have been forcibly abandoned.

In the face of such oppression, Palestinian women like Theeba al-Sabaa have continued to play a pivotal role in protecting their land, particularly when men have been killed or detained by Israeli forces.

“They continue to maintain their leadership role in preserving the family’s agricultural legacy today,” Breijieh said. “This land was historically the primary source of livelihood for families, and a Palestinian cannot leave it voluntarily, no matter the sacrifices.”

He recalled his own grandfather, who went to his fields to bid farewell before dying. “Goodbye, vineyard,” he said to his land.

articles.title: Alex Karp, CEO of America's biggest defence company Palantir, is ‘going’ to Ukraine, says: You and your colleagues are ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is launching a defense technology venture backed by Palantir CEO Alex Karp. For those unaware, Pala.
articles.body: Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is launching a defense technology venture backed by Palantir CEO Alex Karp. For those unaware, Palantir is America's biggest defence technology company. Palantir has several multi-million deals with American government agencies including the Pentagon. Ukrainian defence startup reportedly aims to transform Ukraine’s frontline battlefield innovations into commercial security products for Kyiv and Western allies. Since leaving public office, Fedorov has actively courted Silicon Valley to scale Ukraine’s defense manufacturing footprint. Alongside the new company, he is also reportedly seeking US capital for a defense technology fund targeting autonomous robotics, drone interceptors, and AI-guided missiles.While the financial terms of the investment have not been disclosed, Fedorov’s office said in the statement that Karp will serve as the startup’s first lead investor of the defence startup. In a video shared on X, by Fedorov, Karp is seen praising the initiative, framing it as a way to export Ukraine’s wartime expertise to partner nations. “You and your colleagues are launching a company that I think will be defining for the world,” Karp said, noting that the enterprise could bring Ukraine’s direct combat experience “as a product to allied countries.”Key details remain under wraps, but what makes it importantAll the key operational details about the company remain under wraps. Fedorov’s team has reportedly even declined to disclose the venture’s name, initial product pipeline, or the full scope of Karp’s role, stating only that further phases of the partnership would be announced incrementally.The move comes as Ukraine’s war against Russia fuels rapid iteration in uncrewed systems, battlefield management software, and artificial intelligence. 35-year-old Fedorov spearheaded many of these initiatives during his tenure in government before President Volodymyr Zelenskyy replaced him in July during a broad cabinet reshuffle.“During the full-scale war, our team gained unique experience working with defense technologies in Ukraine and seeing firsthand how technology is transforming modern warfare,” Fedorov said in a statement.The venture also further deepens Fedorov's longstanding ties to US tech leaders. During his government tenure, he frequently interfaced with major American tech executives, recently commending Elon Musk as “the most important tech person and entrepreneur in the world for our country”.Former Google CEO has built one of Ukraine's biggest dronesPalantir CEO Karp is not the only Silicon Valley exec with strong relations with Ukraine. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt too has quietly become an important link between Silicon Valley and Ukraine’s most lethal unmanned strike asset. Schmidt launched Project Eagle, which later became Perennial, with the explicit goal of building a drone that costs less than a used car. Called Hornet, the $5000 unmanned aircraft can carry 5kg of explosives across 200 km in a one-way configuration designed for maximum range rather than recovery.Schmidt did not merely fund this project from a distant office. He actively shaped Perennial as Project Eagle before it evolved into a manufacturing operation capable of producing Hornets at wide scale.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Democrat challenging Mike Lawler won't commit on campaigning with AOC, Mamdani or rejecting DSA
articles.summary: Cait Conley said she won't campaign with Zohran Mamdani or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez but stopped short of rejecting the DSA on national television.
articles.body: Democratic U.S. congressional candidate Cait Conley told CNN's "State of the Union" that she would not campaign alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani or Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., but did not directly answer whether Democrats should reject the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group's influence in New York has become an issue in her bid to unseat Republican Rep. Mike Lawler. Anchor Dana Bash asked Conley whether she would campaign alongside Mamdani or Ocasio-Cortez after noting Lawler has sought to link his opponent to the Democratic Party's socialist wing. "No, Dana, I‘m good up here making the case to the voters in the New York 17th congressional district," Conley said. 'DAMNING SILENCE': SWING-SEAT DEMOCRAT STAYS QUIET AFTER AOC VOICES SUPPORT Lawler's campaign manager, Ciro Riccardi, told Fox News Digital on Sunday that Conley's appearance demonstrated why the campaign has criticized her over debates and accused her of failing to distance herself from the DSA. "Now everyone is seeing why Cait Conley has ducked and dodged debate challenges with Congressman Lawler. She’s incapable of answering direct questions without showing her true colors," he said. "Cait Conley’s refusal to disavow Zohran Mamdani and the DSA is disqualifying. She is just as extreme as the rest and that was exposed today for all to see, including embracing impeachment." Lawler previously told Fox News Digital that he challenged Conley to six debates after her Democratic primary victory, while Conley's campaign said she agreed to two debates hosted by local networks. Bash separately pointed to Rep. Tom Suozzi’s, D-N.Y., calls for his party to confront the DSA and asked Conley whether she agreed. Conley did not directly state whether she believed Democrats should reject the organization, instead discussing political division within both parties. DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’ "I look at what we’re trying to do, which is unite this country where we have seen partisanship to include partisanship within our own party — absolutely divide people to render government dysfunctional," Conley said. "What we have to focus on is how do we bring people together, and right now, what I see coming out of Washington is corruption on both sides, extremism on both sides that is fueling hate, fueling dysfunction." Suozzi has taken a more explicit position toward the socialist organization, telling Fox News Digital in August that Democrats would have to address the DSA's influence and reject its policy positions. "I don't ascribe to any of those ideas at all, and I think that there's very little support for those ideas," Suozzi said. SOCIALISM VS CAPITALISM: HOUSE DEMS CLASH OVER WHAT NY ELECTION RESULTS MEAN FOR PARTY The DSA's national program calls for abolishing I.C.E. and ending detention and deportations. It also advocates redirecting police funding as steps toward "fully abolishing the police and prison system," universal rent control, publicly owned social housing and universal government-funded healthcare. Lawler’s campaign has previously pressed Conley over her relationship with the Democratic Party’s progressive wing after Ocasio-Cortez congratulated Conley on winning the Democratic primary in June. Riccardi at the time challenged Conley to state whether she rejected Ocasio-Cortez and other candidates associated with the party’s left flank. "Which is it, Cait: do you reject AOC and the candidates who want to abolish ICE, defund the police, and tear down our borders, or do you embrace them?" Riccardi said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Conley, a 16-year Army veteran who served on former President Joe Biden's National Security Council, won a crowded Democratic primary in June and is challenging two-term incumbent Lawler in a closely watched Hudson Valley contest that could factor control of the House. Fox News Digital reached out to Conley for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Married couple, young son found dead with gunshot wounds after Los Angeles house fire
articles.summary: US News: A married couple and their young son were found dead with apparent gunshot wounds after a fire broke out at their home in Maywood, Los Angeles County,.
articles.body: A married couple and their young son were found dead with apparent gunshot wounds after a fire broke out at their home in Maywood, Los Angeles County, early Saturday, authorities said.According to the New York Post, citing police, the deaths appeared to be linked to a domestic violence incident, with investigators believing the boy’s father may have been the shooter.The fire was reported at around 2:30 am on September 5, prompting a response from deputies from the East Los Angeles Sheriff’s Station and Los Angeles Fire Department personnel.After firefighters brought the blaze under control, emergency responders searched the house for possible victims. Three people were found unresponsive inside a bedroom — a man and a woman in their late 40s and a boy under the age of 10.All three had apparent gunshot wounds and were pronounced dead at the scene, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said. A firearm was also recovered from the home.“The two adults are married, and the child is their biological child,” the sheriff’s department said in a statement.Authorities have not yet released the identities of the victims, pending notification of their relatives.Officials said there was no threat to the wider public and that the circumstances surrounding the shooting and fire remained under investigation.Anyone with information about the incident has been asked to contact the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Homicide Bureau at (323) 890-5500.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hikers stranded on Mount Shasta after relying on AI to plan trip, sheriff says
articles.summary: Three Roseville hikers used Google's Gemini AI to plan a Mount Shasta climb but ended up stranded overnight in a steep canyon, authorities said.
articles.body: A trio of novice hikers who turned to AI to help plan their climb up California’s Mount Shasta ended up stranded overnight in a steep canyon after their trek went dangerously off course, authorities said. The three young men from Roseville told a Siskiyou County sheriff’s deputy after their rescue that they had relied heavily on Google Gemini for information about the route and what to pack for the trip. That proved to be a "critical misstep," the sheriff’s office said, because Gemini advised them to bring far less food and water than they needed when their planned eight-hour ascent stretched into a multi-day ordeal. CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER The hikers made camp at about 8,400 feet on Saturday, Aug. 29, then set out with daypacks for the summit at 3 a.m. Sunday. They did not reach the top until 7 p.m. — seven hours after the recommended noon turnaround time — leaving them to descend in the dark. About an hour later, the hikers called the sheriff’s office for directions but eventually wandered off the Clear Creek Route and into Mud Creek Canyon. One of the men later fell and injured his knee, stranding the group in the steep canyon overnight. U.S. Forest Service climbing rangers reached the hikers the next morning and treated the injured man. Siskiyou County Search and Rescue volunteers also were sent to help, and everyone made it back to the trailhead safely. MISSOURI DEPUTY AG, MISSING 6 DAYS AFTER SEEKING TO SUMMIT WYOMING'S TALLEST PEAK, IS FOUND ALIVE "It is always advisable to call the local USFS Mount Shasta Ranger Station ahead of your trip to ensure you have the most accurate information, and to never rely solely on AI for your trip planning," the sheriff’s office said. Climbers who have not reached the summit by noon should turn back, the sheriff’s office said, giving themselves — and rescuers, if needed — enough daylight to get off the mountain. Hikers should also carry more than one way to navigate and regularly check that they are still on the correct route rather than depending on a cellphone or GPS device. The Clear Creek Route does not require technical mountaineering, but hikers still need to be fit and prepared for injuries, bad weather or an unexpected night on the mountain, the sheriff’s office said.
