articles.title: 'Total lie’: US rejects Iran’s claim of hitting American vessel in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Middle East News: The US military has rejected Iran’s claim that it struck an unmanned American military vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, calling the report a “total lie.
articles.body: The US military has rejected Iran’s claim that it struck an unmanned American military vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, calling the report a “total lie”, as tensions continued to escalate across the Middle East.State-run Iranian media had claimed that the US vessel was attempting to enter an area that Tehran considers restricted in the strategically important waterway.“The report came from Iranian state media and it’s a total lie,” said Capt. Tim Hawkins, spokesman for US Central Command.The claim came a day after the US said it had struck Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for Iran launching ballistic missiles at US Navy warships. Fighting resumed last week following roughly a month of relative calm.The wider conflict began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28. Although a ceasefire agreement was announced in June, intermittent fighting has continued as efforts to negotiate a lasting settlement have faltered.Iranian Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said the era of “proportionate responses” was over, warning that Iran's retaliation would now be “faster, heavier and more painful.”Israeli strikes kill four in LebanonIsraeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed at least four people and destroyed an empty hospital, according to Lebanon's Health Ministry, in an area that has emerged as a flash point between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah.Two people were killed in strikes on the village of Arabsalim, while two others died in Nabatiyeh, near a strategic hill that Israel said its forces took control of on Thursday.At least 20 people were wounded, including three children and five women, according to Lebanese authorities.The Israeli military said the strikes were carried out in response to a Hezbollah drone attack against Israeli troops in southern Lebanon earlier Sunday. It alleged that Hezbollah had been using the hospital as a command centre.Fighting has declined across much of Lebanon since a ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah took effect more than two months ago, but sporadic clashes and Israeli strikes have continued.More than 110 bodies recovered in GazaIn Gaza City, dozens of Palestinians gathered for a mass funeral after rescue crews recovered the remains of more than 110 people from rubble in the Zeitoun neighbourhood.The victims included at least 70 children, according to reports. Rescue teams spent several days recovering bodies from three families whose homes were destroyed in Israeli strikes earlier in the war.“We are witnessing a painful, heartbreaking scene,” said Mustafa Quzghat, a relative.The bodies were wrapped in white shrouds and laid out in rows, with Palestinian flags placed over them. Some shrouds carried photographs of the deceased.Gaza's Health Ministry says more than 73,650 Palestinians have been killed since the war began. The ministry is part of the Hamas-run government and does not distinguish between civilian and militant deaths in its overall figures.Father, daughter killed in Gaza strikeAn Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle in western Gaza City killed a father and his daughter and wounded at least six others, according to health officials at Shifa Hospital.The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the strike, and it was not immediately clear what the intended target was.Gaza's Health Ministry said Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,344 Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire agreement with Hamas was reached in October.Israel maintains that it targets Hamas and other militants it considers threats and says some strikes are carried out in response to violations of ceasefire arrangements.The Gaza war began after Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel on October 7, 2023, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage.Muslim nations reject proposal to remove PalestiniansForeign ministers from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and five other governments condemned proposals to remove Palestinians from Gaza, saying any such action would violate international law and undermine a US-backed plan aimed at winding down the war.The statement followed a proposal by Israel's national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to encourage Palestinian migration from Gaza. He said the plan would involve Israel paying countries to help cover services for those who leave.Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also said Israel is prepared to facilitate the removal of Palestinians by sea, air or other means, while discussions over the proposals continue.The governments described the statements as “inflammatory” and said they threatened the “legitimate and inalienable rights” of Palestinians and prospects for establishing a Palestinian state.Israel issues holiday travel warningIsrael has also issued a security warning ahead of the Jewish High Holiday season, which begins Friday and is expected to be a busy travel period.Authorities advised Israeli citizens against travelling to Muslim-majority countries including Jordan and Egypt, despite both countries maintaining peace agreements with Israel.Travellers abroad were also urged to exercise caution, including avoiding displaying Jewish symbols such as skullcaps and refraining from speaking Hebrew publicly in certain circumstances.The warnings come as security tensions remain elevated across the region, with fighting and retaliatory strikes continuing despite efforts to contain the wider conflict.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson files for divorce from wife Shannon ‘Summer’ Wilson after 20 years, couple had no prenup; he owns 8.6% stake worth nearly $1B, while she holds 1% valued at $100M
articles.summary: US News: Chip Wilson, the founder of popular athleticwear brand Lululemon, has filed for divorce from his wife and business partner, Shannon ‘Summer’ Wilson, a.
articles.body: Chip Wilson, the founder of popular athleticwear brand Lululemon, has filed for divorce from his wife and business partner, Shannon ‘Summer’ Wilson, after 20 years of marriage. The couple reportedly did not sign a prenuptial agreement, leaving the future division of their considerable assets unclear.Wilson, 71, filed a family legal proceeding in the Supreme Court of British Columbia in April, according to Bloomberg. The American-born entrepreneur, who was raised in Canada and continues to live there, has not publicly detailed the circumstances surrounding the couple’s separation.Those familiar with the matter told the publication that the Wilsons had discussed their separation with friends. The couple have yet to publicly comment on the divorce.Chip Wilson and Shannon Wilson’s connection to LululemonWilson stepped away from Lululemon more than a decade ago. His wife, Shannon ‘Summer’ Wilson, was among the company’s earliest employees and served as its founding lead designer.The couple’s relationship with the brand changed significantly after Wilson became embroiled in controversy over comments he made about Lululemon’s customers and its clothing.In 2013, Wilson made controversial remarks about the bodies and weight of some women who wore the company’s pants. At the time, Lululemon had recalled nearly 17 per cent of its popular black Luon pants after customers complained that the material was see-through.“Quite frankly, some women's bodies just actually don't work for [the pants],” Wilson told Bloomberg in 2013.He went on to discuss the friction caused by women’s thighs and the pressure placed on the fabric over time.The comments sparked widespread backlash. Lululemon subsequently offered customers full refunds or exchanges, while the company’s stock reportedly fell 17 per cent after the controversy.Wilson later apologised for his remarks and departed the company’s board in 2015.Wilson continued to criticise Lululemon after leavingDespite no longer being involved with the company, Wilson continued to speak publicly about Lululemon and its business strategy.In a 2024 interview with Forbes, he criticised the company’s advertising and claimed that promoting what he described as “unhealthy” and “sickly” people was attracting the wrong clientele.Wilson also accused the company of “trying to become like Gap” by appealing to a mass audience rather than maintaining a more exclusive brand identity.“I think the definition of a brand is that you're not everything to everybody,” he said. “You've got to be clear that you don't want certain customers coming in.”He had also publicly criticised what he called the “whole diversity and inclusion thing”, describing it as detrimental to the brand following his departure.Lululemon subsequently distanced itself from Wilson’s comments.“Chip has not been involved with the company since his resignation from the board in 2015 and we are a very different company today,” the company said in a statement to TODAY.The company added that Lululemon was committed to creating an “inclusive, diverse, and welcoming environment” and said it had made considerable progress through its Inclusion, Diversity, Equity and Action initiative.Chip and Shannon Wilson’s Lululemon stakesThe divorce could also have significant financial implications given the couple’s holdings in the company they helped build.According to Bloomberg, Wilson currently owns around 8.6 per cent of Lululemon’s shares, a stake valued at just under $1 billion. His wife reportedly owns approximately a one per cent stake, worth around $100 million.The Wilsons’ reported lack of a prenuptial agreement could therefore make the division of their assets a significant issue as their divorce proceedings move forward.Lululemon faces a difficult periodThe divorce comes as Lululemon’s stock is facing pressure. The company’s shares recently fell 17 per cent in a single week and are reportedly trading near their lowest level in eight years.Meanwhile, former Nike executive Heidi O’Neill is set to take over as Lululemon’s chief executive on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US working on 'peace package' for Ukraine after talks with Putin, Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Europe News: US peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Sunday, stepping up the Trump administration’s .
articles.body: US peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Sunday, stepping up the Trump administration’s renewed push to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year war after holding three hours of talks with Russian president Vladimir Putin in Moscow.The Kyiv meeting was the first visit by Witkoff and Kushner to Ukraine in their capacity as US negotiators. Their Moscow talks on Saturday produced no breakthrough, although Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the meeting as “highly useful”. The White House said further steps would be announced in the coming weeks.Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to pursue a peace agreement but stressed that any settlement would need firm security guarantees and a dignified post-war peace. “Our proposals have been drawn up,” he said ahead of the envoys’ arrival.The Ukrainian president also described his discussions with the US team as “very substantial”. He said the two sides had discussed security and economic guarantees as well as a broader prosperity plan for Ukraine, and expressed hope that the American negotiators would return for further talks.Witkoff struck a similarly positive tone, calling the discussions “substantive” and saying the US was seeking a diplomatic rather than a military resolution to the conflict. Kushner said Washington was working on constructing a “peace package”.The US team also held out the possibility of reviving a trilateral negotiating format involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. European involvement was also expected, with British, French and German national security advisers in Kyiv for discussions.Putin also announced that there was a chance of reaching a peace agreement to end the war in Ukraine on Thursday stating that, “Ultimately...the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict – Russia and Ukraine. Is there a chance [at peace]? In my view, yes, there is.”On the contrary the two sides have recently intensified long-range strikes before the coming of US envoys. Russia has repeatedly targeted Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine has struck Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure in an effort to raise the cost of the war for Moscow.For now the strikes over Moscow and Kyiv on a pause till Monday, for the duration of the US envoys 3-day visit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Photos: UN urges global aid after China, Nepal floods kill over 1,300
articles.summary: UN launches $50m appeal to aid over 84,000 flood survivors in Nepal amid cholera threat and sanitation challenges.
articles.body:
The United Nations’ top official in Nepal has issued an emotional appeal for international aid, warning that survivors of the catastrophic Himalayan flooding last month saw their lives transformed “in one to two minutes”.

The UN Resident Coordinator, Lila Pieters Yahia, said communities along the China-Nepal border were struggling to comprehend the scale of devastation after torrential floods on August 26 tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and hydropower dams.

“You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family,” she told the AFP news agency in Kathmandu. “And you know, this happened in one to two minutes.”

At least 1,384 people were killed and more than 5,500 others remain missing in Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Among the missing are more than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries, including tourists and pilgrims.

Many communities near the epicentre remain cut off, with roads washed away and journeys that once took hours now stretching into days. The UN, working with Nepal’s government, has launched a $50m appeal to support more than 84,000 people affected.

The UN’s Pieters Yahia warned of the risk of cholera and other communicable diseases, citing the deaths of 5,000 cattle and urging urgent investment in sanitation, hygiene and protection for vulnerable women and girls.

“My plea to the international community is: this is the time to help Nepal,” she said. “We can’t leave them alone.”

images.caption: Soldiers rescue a worker from a tunnel during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa district. [Nepal Army via AP Photo]

The flooding that authorities say was likely caused by a glacial collapse last month has killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing, among them about 800 foreigners. [Pedro Pardo/AFP]
Flash flood survivors rest in a relief shelter at Devighat in Nepal's Nuwakot district. [Pedro Pardo/AFP]
The United Nations has launched an appeal for $50m to help more than 84,000 people, saying the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge. [Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo]
Flash flood survivors collect aid from a temporary relief centre at Devighat in Nepal's Nuwakot district. [Pedro Pardo/AFP]
Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has highlighted how leading greenhouse gas emitters have a 'historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal'. [Pedro Pardo / AFP]
He added that the government has officially filed a 'formal climate compensation claim letter' to international partners. [Pedro Pardo / AFP]
Salvaged belongings ins a flash flood-damaged house in Devighat in Nepal. [Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo]

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse remains under investigation, experts say that the frequency and scale of glacier floods have increased as global temperatures have risen. [Pedro Pardo/AFP]

articles.title: Virginia mom placed on child abuse registry for 7 years after letting 5-year-old walk alone
articles.summary: Karyann Parkinson told "Fox & Friends Weekend" Saturday she's appealing her conviction for contributing to the delinquency of a minor in Virginia.
articles.body: A Virginia mom is appealing a criminal charge and her placement on the state’s child abuse and neglect registry after her five-year-old son was stopped by security while walking alone through their gated community. Karyann Parkinson said her son, Sam, had been walking along a familiar neighborhood path past a pond to collect goose feathers when a security guard encountered him and brought him home. Police and Child Protective Services became involved, and Parkinson, who was eight months pregnant at the time, had her six-month jail sentence suspended, but the charge remains. She was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, a first-degree misdemeanor, and was also placed on Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Central Registry for seven years. PARENTS SPEAK OUT AFTER SON WITH AUTISM, 6, WAS SUSPENDED FOR BITING SANDWICH INTO SHAPE OF GUN Parkinson said she understands the shock people feel hearing about a child alone near a body of water, but sought to clarify what happened that day. "I didn't send him to play at the pond," she told "Fox & Friends Weekend." "I sent him down the path that happens to go past the pond to collect goose feathers... I know that a lot of people have seen the headlines and seen 'five-year-old alone at a pond.' And I think if I saw that in isolation, I'd probably be alarmed, too." SAN FRANCISCO DAD QUESTIONED BY PARK RANGERS FOR TEACHING HIS OWN KIDS TENNIS AT PUBLIC COURT "But what this was, was a five-year-old on a pathway that he's very familiar with in his neighborhood that he loves, the only place that he can remember ever living. And it just got turned into this whole situation where a lot of people were suddenly intervening and feeling like this was a really drastic parenting choice," she said. The most difficult part for Parkinson is being on the Child Protective Services registry for so long, she told Fox News. That means she won't be able to volunteer in Sam's classroom until he enters sixth grade. FAMILY STOPPED ALLEGED CHILD KIDNAPPER AS POLICE SAY STAFFING SHORTAGE DELAYED RESPONSE UP TO 40 MINUTES "We need to stop parenting from a place of fear and a place, you know, of obsessing over the unknown or some boogeyman who's going to jump out from behind a bush," Parkinson said. She said her son was "pretty shaken up" after the incident but has since recovered. "We had to do a lot of reassuring him and telling him, 'You didn't do anything wrong,'" Parkinson said. "He would ask me, 'Mom, am I allowed to ride my bike to swim practice? Am I allowed to ride my back to the tennis courts?'" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Now it's just a blip on his radar. It's not really a part of his life anymore," she added.

articles.title: ‘Faster, heavier and more painful’: Iran warns US as sanctions squeeze economy
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran is stepping up efforts to tackle mounting economic problems caused by US sanctions and an oil blockade, while Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Q.
articles.body: Iran is stepping up efforts to tackle mounting economic problems caused by US sanctions and an oil blockade, while Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf has warned that any further attacks will trigger a “faster, heavier and more painful” response.The warning came after US Central Command said it struck three Iranian vessels on Saturday, following the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' launch of ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.The latest escalation comes six months after US and Israeli strikes against Iran. A preliminary ceasefire reached in June has unravelled, while diplomatic efforts to revive negotiations have made little progress.Following the latest strikes, Qalibaf said the United States needed to understand that the rules of the conflict had changed “before it is too late”."From now on, any attack against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response,” he said in a speech published on his Telegram channel.Iran has demonstrated that it retains the ability to target US interests in neighbouring countries and disrupt oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway through which roughly a fifth of global oil supplies flowed before the conflict.Iran opens economic frontWhile military tensions remain high, Iranian officials say the country's economic challenges have become an equally urgent front.Qalibaf said Iran's main battle alongside the military conflict was now focused on production and people's livelihoods. He pointed to currency volatility, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges.He said Iranians could tolerate hardship but not mismanagement or inaction, calling for swift government measures.Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran would respond to US economic pressure through domestic reforms and rejected the idea that sanctions would force Iran to change its policies.“They speak of economic pressure and isolation, ⁠of breaking off financial ties and they think that by pressuring the economy of a country they can change the decisions of its people,” Madanizadeh said.“I have to clarify one point: the responsibility of reforming Iran’s economy is with its government and people, not with the U.S. Treasury."Separately, Economy Ministry deputy Morteza Zamanian said the ministry's “Economic War Headquarters” was intensifying efforts to address problems linked to the war, according to semi-official Tasnim news agency.Oil exports remain under pressureIran is the third-largest producer in OPEC and had been exporting about 90% of its crude through the Kharg Island oil terminal before the war.Those flows have been disrupted since the United States began blocking Iranian oil exports in mid-April.US Central Command said on Sunday that, as of September 6, it had redirected 92 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two as part of efforts to enforce the blockade.Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad said Kharg Island had been hit around 550 times in previous months but remained operational.The comments came after US President Donald Trump on August 31 posted an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being "blown to smithereens". Iranian authorities have warned of a strong response if the island is attacked.US says oil still moving through HormuzIran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has also raised concerns over global energy supplies and fuel prices.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said oil was continuing to pass through the strategic waterway, despite the disruption."Our transits through the Strait are averaging over 9 million barrels a day now, and with the access pipelines that go around the Strait, we're probably two thirds or more of pre-conflict flows. So Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United States Navy is winning that battle," he told CNN.The US military said its Saturday strikes on three Iranian vessels followed ballistic missile launches by the IRGC against two US Navy ships.The IRGC subsequently threatened intensified attacks against US military vessels and later claimed it had targeted the three tankers as well as three US-linked vessels elsewhere.Tasnim reported that four US missiles had struck a tanker near Kharg's anchorage, citing local sources who said there were no casualties and that the crew was being evacuated.Central Command said no American personnel were harmed.Tasnim also reported on Sunday that the IRGC had shot down a US surveillance balloon over Erbil in northern Iraq, describing the incident as part of a broader effort to eliminate US aerial surveillance and early-warning systems in the region.The latest exchanges underscore the widening pressure on Iran, with military confrontation and economic disruption continuing in parallel despite attempts to revive a diplomatic process.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US-backed effort to disarm Iraq’s Iran-linked militias hits setback, experts say
articles.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi vowed to restrict weapons to state control, but militias like Asaib Ahl al-Haq show no credible disarmament evidence.
articles.body: The Trump administration’s push to compel the new Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to dismantle pro-Iran terrorist militias is moving forward — even with some setbacks. As Mideast experts are taking a wait-and-see approach tinged with mild optimism, a senior Iraqi official announced in late August that Baghdad will not treat Sept. 30 as a deadline to disarm the pro-Iran groups known as the Popular Mobilization Units (PMU), also called the Popular Mobilization Forces. The Iraqi government is seeking to exercise control over the rogue state-affiliated militias with a strategy to integrate them into the state apparatus. The radical Iraqi Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, who leads Saraya al-Salam armed group, said in May that he favored integration. Some of the more hardline pro-Iranian regime militias, like Kataeb Hezbollah and Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, declared that they will not disarm or integrate into the state. The official, Qasim al-Araji, security advisor to the prime minister, told Al Iraqiya on Aug. 23 that "Sept. 30 is the date for the international coalition to depart, not the deadline to hand over weapons." The international coalition is the U.S.-led force that defeated the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria during President Trump’s first term. It is unclear why Iraq’s government is walking back the disarmament deadline for the PMU. IRAN'S WAR ON AMERICANS BEGAN DECADES AGO. THESE FAMILIES STILL CARRY THE SCARS A spokesman for the Iraqi embassy declined to comment on the mixed messaging from Iraq’s government and on the timetable for dissolving or integrating the PMU. Just days before al-Araji’s announcement, a representative of the Iraqi government sent Fox News Digital a statement: "Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi: All political forces fully agree on moving forward with restricting weapons to state control, and work is underway on mechanisms for surrendering weapons and bringing this issue to a complete end." Al-Zaidi told the Baghdad Dialogue Conference at the same time that "all political forces agree on moving forward to ensure that all arms remain under state authority and on developing mechanisms for the handover of weapons. There are no intentions or prospects of any military confrontation, and we will not allow Iraq’s enemies to exploit any opportunity. The presence of weapons outside state authority creates an environment that discourages investment, which is unacceptable because it does not serve the interests of Iraqis." In May, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Ali Maarij Al-Bahadly, Iraq’s Deputy Minister of Oil, because he, according to the designation, "abuses his position to facilitate the diversion of oil to be sold for the benefit of the Iranian regime and its proxy militias in Iraq." Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said at the time "Like a rogue gang, the Iranian regime is pillaging resources that rightfully belong to the Iraqi people," adding "Treasury will not stand idly by as Iran's military exploits Iraqi oil to fund terrorism against the United States and our partners." In late August, the UAE's The National paper reported that "Iraq's anti-corruption body announced that deputy oil minister, Al-Bahadly, was sentenced to seven years in prison and fined millions of dollars for corruption. Reacting to reports that Iran approved passage of Iraqi oil tankers via the Strait of Hormuz, former U.S. ambassador and Mideast analyst, Alberto Fernandez claimed that "the profit from that Iraqi oil goes, in part, to pay for Iran’s own Iraqi militias/death squads on the Iraqi government’s payroll." An Iraqi government spokesman dismissed Fernandez's comments, telling Fox News Digital, "That is not accurate." TRUMP’S COUNTERTERRORISM STRATEGY SCORES BIG WINS AGAINST GLOBAL TERROR THREATS A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "Iraq has embarked on a new direction under the leadership of Prime Minister Al-Zaidi in full partnership with the United States. As President Trump made clear when he hosted Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s historic July 14 visit, the United States strongly supports his vision to ensure a brighter future for all Iraqis free from terrorism, to prevent attacks in and from Iraqi territory, and to deliver a strong and mutually beneficial U.S.-Iraq partnership." Entifadh Qanbar, a former spokesman for the deputy prime minister of Iraq during the George W. Bush administration, told Fox News Digital: "We were all hoping that Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi would take decisive action against the militias, especially after his visit to the White House and the widespread praise he received from President Trump. I was always skeptical, very skeptical, but I believed he deserved a chance." Qanbar added that "Initially, some militias such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali (sanctioned by the U.S.) merely issued statements claiming they would hand over their weapons. There has been no credible evidence that they have actually disarmed." IRAN’S GUTTED RANKS LEAVE LOYALISTS FILLING CRITICAL POSTS — WITH ONE GLARING PROBLEM Qanbar claimed that "any remaining hope was further diminished after IRGC [Islamic Republic Guard Corps] Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani visited Baghdad. According to multiple reports, he instructed militia leaders to slow down any discussion of disarmament, reject the September 30 deadline, and maintain their weapons as part of Iran’s broader regional deterrence strategy." When asked about Iraqi state efforts to dismantle the PMU, Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior non-resident fellow at the New Lines Institute in Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital that "the Iraqi government is trying. It genuinely carried out some moves.
